My more recent attempts at gardening are in the southern US with heavy Spring rains followed by drought and intense heat.

We have seen some success with tomatoes using five-gallon buckets (with drainage holes in bottom and in lower three inches of sides). The soil mix was local sandy loam, aged cow manure, and compost. A teaspoon of "plant crack" (even parts Epsom salt, bone meal, and blood meal) was mixed into the soil at the bottom of hole at time of transplanting. A small handful of baked-and-ground eggshells was mixed into that soil as well. After planting seedling deep with the topmost leaves above ground, finely-crushed eggshells were sprinkled around top of soil. Then, the plants were heavily mulched. Plant crack was sprinkled in a ring around plants every two or three weeks.

A concerted effort was made to keep the plants evenly watered with collected rain water (if possible) or city water that had sat in a bucket for at least one day.

The bucket system worked well when we had limited space. That was until we had huge rains following a drought. All of the tomatoes split open and the roots stressed.

An experiment this year seems to be working well. One caveat is that the tomatoes were planted midsummer. I would like to try this in the Spring.

The experiment in nontilled soil mulched with wood chips and pine straw:

Establish pole beans, morning glories, and moonflowers along a trellis fence. Beside the established beans, plant a row of tomato seedlings (that I grew from seeds) directly in nontilled soil, but with plant crack, aged manure, and ground eggshells mixed with soil in bottom of planting holes. Tomato seedlings are planted deep. Closely plant two rows of bush beans or cow peas along row of tomatoes. Sprinkle crushed eggshells and ground eggshells on top of soil. Mulch with pine straw. Periodically, water deeply at ground level.
